title: The Reform Almost Nobody Can Name
hook: About 2% of those polled could name proportional representation unprompted. Told what it does, half backed it — opinion on institutions stays latent until someone describes them.
key_points: US House elections use single-member, winner-take-all districts: one seat per district, awarded to whoever gets the most votes.
Proportional representation elects several members per district, roughly in proportion to each party's vote share — the system most of the world's democracies now use.
In a poll by Fix Our House and New America, half of 1,000 respondents backed proportional representation, about a quarter opposed, and a third were unsure.
Only ~2% named it unprompted and just a quarter knew alternatives to a two-party system existed — support appears once the idea is explained.
54% also supported enlarging the House by 150 seats — advocates call expansion essential, since without it incumbents would be voting themselves out of seats.
Read with care: the poll was commissioned by reform advocates, and Pew notes reforms often lose support as they move from theory to practice.
content_html: Ask Americans about proportional representation and almost none of them will recognize the phrase — roughly 2% of respondents in a new poll could name it unprompted. Explain what it does, and half of them say they like it. That gap is the interesting finding, and it is really a lesson about how public opinion on institutions works.
extra_html:
The US elects its House from single-member, winner-take-all districts: one seat per district, to whoever collects the most votes. Proportional representation instead elects several representatives from a larger district and splits those seats roughly in line with each party's vote share, so a party with a quarter of the vote wins about a quarter of the seats. It is now the most widely used system among the world's democracies; the US, Canada, and Australia are among the holdouts.

NPR's Ashley Lopez reported on a survey of 1,000 respondents by the advocacy group Fix Our House and the think tank New America: half supported proportional representation, roughly a quarter opposed, and a third were unsure. New America's Lee Drutman said the breadth surprised him — 6 in 10 Trump voters with an opinion backed it — and that support held when pollsters walked people through the trade-offs, including coalition governments that govern less efficiently and the prospect of more small parties. On that last worry, Drutman said, respondents mostly shrugged: they already consider the existing parties fairly extreme. A separate question found 54% support for adding 150 seats to the House, which Fix Our House's Dustin Wahl called a precondition for any bill, since expansion is what spares incumbents from having to vote themselves out of a seat. Two caveats matter for reading any of this. The poll was commissioned by people who favor the reform, and, as Pew's Jocelyn Kiley points out, voters rarely know the details of a proposed reform in advance and enthusiasm often fades once a change "moves from theory to practice" and people ask how it would affect them specifically. What the numbers plausibly show is not a mandate but an opening — an electorate frustrated enough to listen to alternatives it has never had described to it.

related.title: Districts & Gerrymandering
related.hook: Where you draw the lines on a map can decide an election before a single vote is cast — which is exactly what gerrymandering exploits.

related.hook: Parties are how scattered voters become an organized choice. Whether a country has two big ones or a dozen shapes how its whole politics feels.

related.hook: Many voters no longer back a candidate they admire — they vote to keep the other party out. That 'negative partisanship' can make even scandal forgivable.

flashcards.prompt: How does proportional representation differ from the system used for US House elections?

choices.text: It elects multiple members per district in rough proportion to each party's vote share, instead of one winner-take-all seat
It lets voters rank candidates but still awards one seat per district
It replaces districts with a nationwide popular vote for president

flashcards.explanation_html: US House districts are single-member and winner-take-all. PR uses multi-member districts and allocates their seats by vote share.

flashcards.prompt: Why do advocates argue House expansion must accompany a switch to proportional representation?
flashcards.back_html: Without extra seats, sitting members would effectively be voting themselves out of office. A 150-seat cushion means incumbents' own chances are untouched, which advocates say is what makes a bill viable.

flashcards.prompt: What should make you cautious about reading this poll as settled public demand?

choices.text: It was commissioned by reform advocates, and few respondents knew the idea before being told about it
The sample contained only voters from one political party
Respondents were never asked about any trade-offs

flashcards.explanation_html: Pew's Jocelyn Kiley notes detailed knowledge of reforms is rare and support often erodes once a reform "moves from theory to practice."
